# Translations 

the `translation` class indicates that a code block will contain translation
exercises that require symbolizing natural language sentences.

## Propositional Translations

For propositional translation exercises, provide an English sentence
and a list of accepted translations. For instance,

    :::translate{id="3.1" variant="prop"}
    People want to know what's going on and questions are unavoidable
    - P/\Q
    :::

generates

:::translate{id="3.1"}
People want to know what's going on and questions are unavoidable
- P/\Q
:::

To complete it, type the answer into the text box. Carnap will check
the answer after a pause in typing. Propositional translations are
considered correct if they are logically equivalent to the original
answer. So for example, `Q/\P` will be accepted above.

If you say `variant="prop"`, Carnap rejects quantifiers, identity, and predicates with individual arguments in both
solutions and submitted answers. `prop` is the default and does not
have to be specified.

## First-Order Translation

It is also possible to create first-order translation problems using
the variant `first-order`, thus:

    :::translate{id="3.2" variant="first-order"}
    Everything is fine
    - AxF(x)
    :::

with the result:

:::translate{id="3.2" variant="first-order"}
Everything is fine
- AxF(x)
:::

These are completed as above. Carnap conducts a proof search
attempting to show the provided answer equivalent to the model
solution(s). Equivalence of first-order sentences is undecidable, so
this does not always provide a reliable answer. In some cases.

## Exact Translations

Using the variant `exact`, you can also create "translations" that don't accept
logically equivalent answers. These may be useful if you wish to, for example,
ask a student what the missing premise in some inference is. So, for example
you might write

    :::translation{id="3.3" variant=exact}
    To make a modus ponens inference with P→Q, you need...

    - P
    :::

to generate:

:::translation{id="3.3" variant=exact}
    To make a modus ponens inference with P→Q, you need...

- P
:::

Exact translations use the same syntax as `variant=prop` by default,
but can be configured to use alternative systems.

## Systems

The way that formulas are parsed can also be customized. This is done by
setting the `system` attribute to indicate which formal system you are drawing
your syntax from. So for example, 

    :::translation{id="3.4" variant="first-order" system="forallx-magnus"}
    Everything is totally bananas

    - @x (Tx & Bx)
    :::

will generate:

:::translation{id="3.4" variant="first-order" system="forallx-magnus"}
Everything is totally bananas

- @x (Tx & Bx)
:::

## Advanced usage

#### Multiple Solutions

If you wish to allow students to find one translation of a sentence that admits
several formalizations, you can use a comma-separated list of admissible
solutions. So, 

    :::translation{id="3.5"}
    Jack jumped the fence and was caught by the watchman or got away.
    - (P /\ Q) \/ R, P/\(Q\/R)
    :::

generates 

:::translation{id="3.5"}
Jack jumped the fence and was caught by the watchman or got away.
- (P /\ Q) \/ R, P/\(Q\/R)
:::

#### Options and Attributes

The following are allowed as space-separated values of `options`:

<div class="table">

Name                     Effect
------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------
`nocheck`                Disables checking solutions
`checksyntax`            When `exam` is active, blocks submission of syntactically incorrect work
------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

#### Translation tests

Finally, you can impose one or more extra tests on a translation. This is done
by setting the `tests` attribute to indicate which tests you wish to require
the translation to pass. The available tests for propositional translations are

<div class="table">

Name                     Effect
------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------
`CNF`                    Requires conjunctive normal form
`DNF`                    Requires disjunctive normal form
`maxCon:N`               Requires that the translation contain N or fewer connectives
`maxNot:N`               Requires that the translation contain N or fewer negations
`maxAnd:N`               Requires that the translation contain N or fewer conjunctions
`maxIff:N`               Requires that the translation contain N or fewer biconditionals
`maxIf:N`                Requires that the translation contain N or fewer conditionals
`maxOr:N`                Requires that the translation contain N or fewer disjunctions
`maxFalse:N`             Requires that the translation contain N or fewer falsity constants
`maxAtom:N`              Requires that the translation contain N or fewer atomic sentences
------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>
 
The available tests for first-order translations are all the propositional
tests, plus:

<div class="table">

Name                     Effect
------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------
`PNF`                    Requires prenex normal form
------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

When using multiple tests, their names must be separated by spaces, so for
example,

    :::translation{id="3.6" variant="first-order" tests="PNF maxNeg:0"}
    Nothing is not bananas.

    - ~Ex~F(x)
    :::

will generate:

:::translation{id="3.6" variant="first-order" tests="PNF maxNeg:0"}
Nothing is not bananas.
- ~Ex~F(x)
:::

#### Partial Solutions

It's possible to include a partial solution to a translation problem,
by including the partial solution as a value for `starter`. So for
example,

    :::translation{id="3.7" variant="first-order" options="nocheck" starter="For all x, x is fine"}
    Everything is fine
    - AxF(x)
    :::

Generates

:::translation{id="3.7" variant="first-order" options="nocheck" starter="For all x, x is fine"}
Everything is fine
- AxF(x)
:::
